title: CTS Psalms — Unit 8: Psalm 28, When God Is Silent

blocks.en: 📖 The Book of Psalms — Unit 8: Psalm 28, When God Is Silent
blocks.es_reference: 📖 El Libro de los Salmos — Unidad 8: Salmo 28, Cuando Dios Calla

blocks.en: Professor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers
blocks.es_reference: Profesor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers

blocks.en: "To You I will cry, O Lord my Rock: do not be silent to me." — Psalm 28:1 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "A ti clamaré, oh Jehová; Roca mía, no te desentiendas de mí." — Salmo 28:1 (RVG)

blocks.en: 1. The Pain of Silence
blocks.es_reference: 1. El Dolor del Silencio

blocks.en: I do not care much for thunderstorms. The lightning around here can do real damage; one strike a while back knocked out three modems in our house. But the most irritating part comes when I am in the middle of a program and the screen suddenly goes blank, and a message pops up saying the signal cannot be received. There I sit with a fine dish, a television, and all the wires — and nothing but silence. We live with constant, pervasive background noise, and we have grown so accustomed to it that we feel uncomfortable without it. Silence can be painful, and never more so than when it is the silence of God.
blocks.es_reference: No me gustan mucho las tormentas eléctricas. Los rayos por aquí pueden causar verdadero daño; uno hace un tiempo dejó sin funcionar tres módems en nuestra casa. Pero la parte más irritante llega cuando estoy en medio de un programa y la pantalla de pronto se pone en blanco, y aparece un mensaje que dice que no se puede recibir la señal. Allí me quedo con una buena antena, un televisor y todos los cables — y nada más que silencio. Vivimos con un ruido de fondo constante y omnipresente, y nos hemos acostumbrado tanto a él que nos sentimos incómodos sin él. El silencio puede ser doloroso, y nunca tanto como cuando es el silencio de Dios.

blocks.en: Oh, how we would like to be like Moses, to whom God spoke from a burning bush; or like Elijah, who carried on a running conversation with the Lord; or like Christ, who often went off alone to be with His Father. Instead there are seasons when we cry out and heaven seems quiet. The trials we face are real — cancer is real, divorce is real, death is real, pain is real — and in the middle of them the silence of God can leave us upset, confused, and heartbroken, our faith suddenly up for grabs. Psalm 28 is the prayer of a man in exactly that place: "To You I will cry, O LORD my Rock: do not be silent to me." Why is God sometimes silent? Scripture offers at least three answers.
blocks.es_reference: Oh, cómo quisiéramos ser como Moisés, a quien Dios habló desde una zarza ardiente; o como Elías, que mantenía una conversación continua con el Señor; o como Cristo, que a menudo se apartaba a solas para estar con Su Padre. En cambio hay temporadas en que clamamos y el cielo parece callado. Las pruebas que enfrentamos son reales — el cáncer es real, el divorcio es real, la muerte es real, el dolor es real — y en medio de ellas el silencio de Dios puede dejarnos angustiados, confundidos y con el corazón roto, con la fe de pronto en juego. El Salmo 28 es la oración de un hombre en ese mismo lugar: "A ti clamaré, oh Jehová; Roca mía, no te desentiendas de mí." ¿Por qué calla Dios a veces? La Escritura ofrece al menos tres respuestas.

blocks.en: 2. Silent Because We Must Experience Him
blocks.es_reference: 2. Calla Porque Debemos Experimentarle

blocks.en: John 4:24 (NKJV): "God is Spirit, and those who worship Him must worship in spirit and truth."
blocks.es_reference: Juan 4:24 (RVG): "Dios es Espíritu; y los que le adoran, en espíritu y en verdad es necesario que adoren."

blocks.en: We experience the world through five senses — sight and hearing, touch, taste, and smell. A newborn must learn to use them; his eyes do not yet focus and he does not understand sound. But none of those senses reaches God, for God is Spirit. We can only use the language of the senses to describe Him to others — we say He "speaks" to us, that we keep our "eyes" on Him. To truly experience God, we must learn a different kind of attention. Think of young Samuel, given to the Lord and raised in the temple under Eli. One night he heard a voice and ran to Eli, who had not called him. It happened again, and a third time, until Eli understood and told the boy, "When you hear it again, say, 'Speak, LORD, for Your servant is listening.'" That posture — quiet, attentive, ready — is how the soul learns to hear God.
blocks.es_reference: Experimentamos el mundo por medio de cinco sentidos — la vista y el oído, el tacto, el gusto y el olfato. Un recién nacido debe aprender a usarlos; sus ojos aún no enfocan y no entiende el sonido. Pero ninguno de esos sentidos alcanza a Dios, porque Dios es Espíritu. Solo podemos usar el lenguaje de los sentidos para describirlo a otros — decimos que nos "habla," que tenemos los "ojos" puestos en Él. Para experimentar verdaderamente a Dios, debemos aprender otra clase de atención. Piense en el joven Samuel, entregado al Señor y criado en el templo bajo Elí. Una noche oyó una voz y corrió a Elí, que no lo había llamado. Sucedió otra vez, y una tercera, hasta que Elí entendió y le dijo al niño: "Cuando la oigas de nuevo, di: Habla, Jehová, porque tu siervo oye." Esa postura — quieta, atenta, dispuesta — es como el alma aprende a oír a Dios.

blocks.en: There is a true story of a man born blind who grew up, lived on his own, and played hockey. Then he fell in love, and his sweetheart learned of an operation that might give him sight. He had the surgery, but when the bandages came off he was terrified. His brain had never processed sight, and the flood of sensation overwhelmed him; he shut his eyes tight and asked, "Is this what sight is like?" It took months to learn to use what his eyes were now giving him. So it is with God. When we want to experience Him, we usually close our eyes and find a quiet place, turning off the other senses that distract us, so that the spiritual sense can learn to perceive Him.
blocks.es_reference: Hay una historia real de un hombre que nació ciego, creció, vivió por su cuenta y jugaba hockey. Luego se enamoró, y su novia supo de una operación que podría darle la vista. Se operó, pero cuando le quitaron las vendas quedó aterrado. Su cerebro nunca había procesado la vista, y la avalancha de sensaciones lo abrumó; cerró los ojos con fuerza y preguntó: "¿Así es la vista?" Le tomó meses aprender a usar lo que ahora le daban sus ojos. Así es con Dios. Cuando queremos experimentarle, solemos cerrar los ojos y buscar un lugar tranquilo, apagando los demás sentidos que distraen, para que el sentido espiritual aprenda a percibirle.

blocks.en: 3. The Grace Hidden in Silence
blocks.es_reference: 3. La Gracia Escondida en el Silencio

blocks.en: Catherine Marshall's Surrendered Dreams: At fifteen Catherine Marshall sensed God asking her to surrender her dreams to Him — her longing to attend Agnes Scott College and to marry the right man someday. The Depression had left her pastor father hundreds of dollars short of the tuition. One night her mother found her sobbing across her bed and said, "Every problem has a solution. Let's ask God." Catherine prayed, "Lord, I turn this dream over to You. I give it up. You decide." She later wrote that the price of a relationship with God is the dropping of all our masks — we come to Him with stark honesty, "as we are," or not at all. God provided; she went to Agnes Scott, and there she met and married Peter Marshall, later chaplain of the U.S. Senate. Years on, at the peak of their ministry, she was struck with tuberculosis and confined to bed for two years. There Psalm 23 came alive: she was being made to "lie down in green pastures." When healing finally came, and later when Peter died suddenly, she had learned to lean on the God who had been training her in the quiet all along.
blocks.es_reference: Los Sueños Entregados de Catherine Marshall: A los quince años Catherine Marshall sintió que Dios le pedía entregarle sus sueños — su anhelo de asistir al Agnes Scott College y de casarse algún día con el hombre correcto. La Depresión había dejado a su padre, pastor, cientos de dólares corto para la matrícula. Una noche su madre la halló sollozando sobre su cama y le dijo: "Todo problema tiene solución. Pidámoslo a Dios." Catherine oró: "Señor, te entrego este sueño. Lo suelto. Tú decides." Más tarde escribió que el precio de una relación con Dios es soltar todas nuestras máscaras — venimos a Él con franca honestidad, "tal como somos," o no venimos. Dios proveyó; fue al Agnes Scott, y allí conoció y se casó con Peter Marshall, luego capellán del Senado de los Estados Unidos. Años después, en la cumbre de su ministerio, la golpeó la tuberculosis y quedó dos años confinada a la cama. Allí cobró vida el Salmo 23: era hecha "descansar en lugares de delicados pastos." Cuando al fin llegó la sanidad, y luego cuando Peter murió de repente, había aprendido a apoyarse en el Dios que la había estado formando en el silencio todo el tiempo.

blocks.en: This is the secret hidden inside God's silence: it is often grace. It is one of His ways of getting our attention when we are distracted by a thousand other things. The very pain of the silence stirs a hunger that pushes us toward Him, into the arms of Jesus Christ — who, by the way, is the only person who ever lived who heard the total, deafening silence of God. Nailed to the cross, He cried, "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" and that cry was answered by nothing but silence, so that ours never need be.
blocks.es_reference: Este es el secreto escondido dentro del silencio de Dios: a menudo es gracia. Es una de Sus maneras de captar nuestra atención cuando estamos distraídos por mil otras cosas. El dolor mismo del silencio despierta un hambre que nos empuja hacia Él, a los brazos de Jesucristo — quien, por cierto, es la única persona que jamás vivió que oyó el silencio total y ensordecedor de Dios. Clavado en la cruz, clamó: "Dios mío, Dios mío, ¿por qué me has desamparado?" y aquel clamor fue respondido con nada más que silencio, para que el nuestro nunca tenga que serlo.

blocks.en: 4. Silent Because We Haven't Tuned In
blocks.es_reference: 4. Calla Porque No Hemos Sintonizado

blocks.en: Psalm 46:10 (NKJV): "Be still, and know that I am God."
blocks.es_reference: Salmo 46:10 (RVG): "Estad quietos, y conoced que yo soy Dios."

blocks.en: When I listen to the radio, I am tuned almost always to one station. My sons once wondered why I had never set the other channels; the truth is I keep it on the one I want to hear. We live in a world of distractions, with so many labor-saving devices that we are about to wear ourselves out keeping them all running. We do not know what to do with silence; if it gets too quiet we reach for the television or the radio. But to hear the voice of God we have to listen through the silence. And God does not usually shout. The Scripture says He speaks in a still, small voice — a voice easily drowned out by the cacophony of the world's seductive noise.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando escucho la radio, estoy sintonizado casi siempre en una sola emisora. Mis hijos una vez se preguntaron por qué nunca había programado los otros canales; la verdad es que la dejo en el que quiero oír. Vivimos en un mundo de distracciones, con tantos aparatos que ahorran trabajo que estamos a punto de agotarnos manteniéndolos todos en marcha. No sabemos qué hacer con el silencio; si se pone demasiado quieto, buscamos el televisor o la radio. Pero para oír la voz de Dios tenemos que escuchar a través del silencio. Y Dios por lo general no grita. La Escritura dice que habla en un silbo apacible y delicado — una voz fácilmente ahogada por la cacofonía del ruido seductor del mundo.

blocks.en: A man once lost his valuable watch in an ice house. His fellow workers searched diligently, combing every inch of the place, but could not find it. A little boy heard about the search and, during the lunch hour, slipped inside and quickly came out with the watch. The amazed men asked, "How did you find it?" He said, "I simply went in, closed the door, lay down quietly on the floor, and listened. After a while I could hear the tick, tick, tick of the watch." Some things can only be heard in stillness.
blocks.es_reference: Un hombre una vez perdió su valioso reloj en una casa de hielo. Sus compañeros lo buscaron con diligencia, peinando cada rincón del lugar, pero no lo hallaron. Un niño oyó de la búsqueda y, a la hora del almuerzo, se metió y salió enseguida con el reloj. Los hombres asombrados preguntaron: "¿Cómo lo hallaste?" Dijo: "Simplemente entré, cerré la puerta, me acosté quieto en el suelo, y escuché. Al cabo de un rato pude oír el tic, tic, tic del reloj." Algunas cosas solo se oyen en la quietud.

blocks.en: 5. Tuned to His Frequency
blocks.es_reference: 5. Sintonizados en Su Frecuencia

blocks.en: Another reason we miss God's voice is that our ears are not tuned to His frequency. It is not that He is silent; it is that we have forgotten what His voice sounds like, and so we miss it.
blocks.es_reference: Otra razón por la que perdemos la voz de Dios es que nuestros oídos no están sintonizados en Su frecuencia. No es que Él calle; es que hemos olvidado cómo suena Su voz, y por eso la perdemos.

blocks.en: The Cricket on Fifth Avenue: In the late nineteenth century at Dartmouth College, a young American Indian student roomed with another classmate, who over Christmas invited him home to New York City. The visitor had never seen a great city, and one day as they walked down Fifth Avenue he was amazed at the crowds, the carriages, the horses, and the roar of city sounds. Suddenly he stopped. "Listen. Do you hear it? A cricket." "Are you crazy?" his friend said. But the young man crossed the street, ran up the steps of an apartment building, leaned into a flower box — and there was the cricket. His ear was simply tuned to that frequency. So we may learn to tune our hearts to God, turning on our receiving set each morning by asking, "Lord, what is before me to do today?" and then listening, expecting good, because God is broadcasting His good to us constantly.
blocks.es_reference: El Grillo en la Quinta Avenida: A fines del siglo diecinueve, en el Dartmouth College, un joven estudiante indígena americano compartía cuarto con otro compañero, quien en Navidad lo invitó a su casa en la ciudad de Nueva York. El visitante nunca había visto una gran ciudad, y un día, mientras caminaban por la Quinta Avenida, quedó asombrado de las multitudes, los carruajes, los caballos y el rugido de los sonidos de la ciudad. De pronto se detuvo. "Escucha. ¿Lo oyes? Un grillo." "¿Estás loco?" dijo su amigo. Pero el joven cruzó la calle, subió corriendo los escalones de un edificio, se inclinó sobre una jardinera — y allí estaba el grillo. Su oído sencillamente estaba sintonizado en esa frecuencia. Así podemos aprender a sintonizar el corazón con Dios, encendiendo nuestro receptor cada mañana al preguntar: "Señor, ¿qué tengo por delante para hacer hoy?" y luego escuchando, esperando el bien, porque Dios nos transmite Su bien constantemente.

blocks.en: 6. Silent Because We Have Turned Away
blocks.es_reference: 6. Calla Porque Nos Hemos Apartado

blocks.en: There is a third reason for the silence, and it is the hardest: sometimes we have turned away. When Adam sinned in the garden, he hid himself, and God came calling, "Adam, where are you?" — not because God had lost him, but because Adam had hidden. Unconfessed sin, or a settled pattern of sin, plugs up our ears so that even when God is speaking we cannot hear Him.
blocks.es_reference: Hay una tercera razón para el silencio, y es la más dura: a veces nos hemos apartado. Cuando Adán pecó en el huerto, se escondió, y Dios vino llamando: "Adán, ¿dónde estás?" — no porque Dios lo hubiera perdido, sino porque Adán se había escondido. El pecado no confesado, o un patrón arraigado de pecado, tapa nuestros oídos de modo que aun cuando Dios habla no podemos oírle.

blocks.en: In college I came down with a severe case of strep throat, so bad that the infection spread to my inner ears and I was actually going deaf. At one point the doctors removed astonishingly large plugs of wax from my ears — and suddenly I could hear again. Sin works like that. Left unchecked, it spreads like an infection and stops up the ears of faith. But God in His graciousness convicts us, and when we act on that conviction, turning to Him in repentance and confessing our sin, He graciously unstops our ears. Then we discover He had been speaking to us all along; we simply could not — or would not — hear Him.
blocks.es_reference: En la universidad me dio un caso severo de infección de garganta, tan grave que la infección se extendió a mis oídos internos y de hecho me estaba quedando sordo. En cierto momento los médicos me sacaron tapones de cera asombrosamente grandes de los oídos — y de pronto pude oír otra vez. Así obra el pecado. Sin control, se extiende como una infección y tapa los oídos de la fe. Pero Dios en Su gracia nos convence, y cuando actuamos sobre esa convicción, volviéndonos a Él en arrepentimiento y confesando nuestro pecado, Él misericordiosamente destapa nuestros oídos. Entonces descubrimos que nos había estado hablando todo el tiempo; sencillamente no podíamos — o no queríamos — oírle.

blocks.en: 7. Sowing, Reaping, and the Chastening of a Father
blocks.es_reference: 7. Sembrar, Segar, y la Disciplina de un Padre

blocks.en: Two of God's laws help us understand His silence. The first is the law of sowing and reaping: "whatever a man sows, that he will also reap" (Galatians 6:7). This is a universal law. Even the thief on the cross, fully forgiven, still had to bear the consequences of his sinful life. Forgiveness restores the relationship; it does not always cancel the harvest. The second is the law of chastening, which applies only to God's children. When David sinned, the prophet Nathan told him he would not die, but that the child born to him would. David prayed and fasted seven days, and still God was silent and the child died (2 Samuel 12). Sometimes God's silence toward us is the loving discipline of a Father who is correcting a course we cannot yet see is wrong.
blocks.es_reference: Dos de las leyes de Dios nos ayudan a entender Su silencio. La primera es la ley de la siembra y la cosecha: "todo lo que el hombre sembrare, eso también segará" (Gálatas 6:7). Esta es una ley universal. Aun el ladrón en la cruz, plenamente perdonado, todavía tuvo que llevar las consecuencias de su vida pecaminosa. El perdón restaura la relación; no siempre cancela la cosecha. La segunda es la ley del castigo paternal, que se aplica solo a los hijos de Dios. Cuando David pecó, el profeta Natán le dijo que no moriría, pero que el niño que le nacería sí. David oró y ayunó siete días, y aun así Dios calló y el niño murió (2 Samuel 12). A veces el silencio de Dios hacia nosotros es la disciplina amorosa de un Padre que corrige un rumbo que aún no vemos que está errado.

blocks.en: Psalm 139:23-24 (NKJV): "Search me, O God, and know my heart; try me, and know my anxieties; and see if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting."
blocks.es_reference: Salmo 139:23-24 (RVG): "Examíname, oh Dios, y conoce mi corazón; pruébame y conoce mis pensamientos; y ve si hay en mí camino de perversidad, y guíame en el camino eterno."

blocks.en: That is the prayer for a season of silence: not to demand that God speak on our terms, but to ask Him to show us what is wrong and how to make it right.
blocks.es_reference: Esa es la oración para una temporada de silencio: no exigir que Dios hable en nuestros términos, sino pedirle que nos muestre qué está mal y cómo enmendarlo.

blocks.en: 8. Turning Back to the God Who Speaks
blocks.es_reference: 8. Volver al Dios que Habla

blocks.en: The great Scottish teacher William Barclay observed that real turning, real repentance, always involves two movements: a turning from something and a turning toward something. We turn from the sin and noise and distraction that stopped our ears, and we turn toward the God who has been speaking all along. There were four hundred silent years between the last prophet and John the Baptist — and then God spoke His final and fullest Word, His Son. He is never as silent as He seems.
blocks.es_reference: El gran maestro escocés William Barclay observó que el verdadero volverse, el verdadero arrepentimiento, siempre implica dos movimientos: un apartarse de algo y un volverse hacia algo. Nos apartamos del pecado, el ruido y la distracción que taparon nuestros oídos, y nos volvemos hacia el Dios que ha estado hablando todo el tiempo. Hubo cuatrocientos años de silencio entre el último profeta y Juan el Bautista — y entonces Dios habló Su Palabra final y más plena, Su Hijo. Él nunca calla tanto como parece.

blocks.en: If you are in a season when heaven seems quiet, do not conclude that God has abandoned you. He may be teaching you to experience Him beyond the senses; He may be inviting you to be still and tune your heart to His frequency; He may be calling you, like Adam, back from a place you have wandered. In every case the answer is the same: draw near. Be still. Confess what needs confessing. And say with Samuel, "Speak, LORD, for Your servant is listening." The God who broke four hundred years of silence with the cry of a newborn in Bethlehem has not stopped speaking to those who will quiet themselves to hear.
blocks.es_reference: Si está en una temporada en que el cielo parece callado, no concluya que Dios le ha abandonado. Tal vez le esté enseñando a experimentarle más allá de los sentidos; tal vez le esté invitando a estar quieto y a sintonizar el corazón en Su frecuencia; tal vez le esté llamando, como a Adán, de regreso de un lugar a donde se ha extraviado. En todo caso la respuesta es la misma: acérquese. Esté quieto. Confiese lo que haya que confesar. Y diga con Samuel: "Habla, Jehová, porque tu siervo oye." El Dios que rompió cuatrocientos años de silencio con el clamor de un recién nacido en Belén no ha dejado de hablar a los que se aquietan para oír.

mc.stem: The lesson opens with a screen going silent when the signal is lost. What does this picture about God's silence?
options: That God never speaks at all
That God's silence can be painful and disorienting, like losing a signal we depend on
mc.why: The lesson opens with a screen going silent when the signal is lost — picturing how God's silence can pain and disorient us.

mc.stem: According to the lesson, why has silence become painful for modern people?
options: We have grown so accustomed to constant noise that we feel uncomfortable without it
mc.why: Silence feels painful because we have grown so used to constant noise that we are uncomfortable without it.

mc.stem: Which three biblical figures does the lesson cite as those we wish we could imitate in hearing God?
mc.why: We wish we could hear God like Moses, Elijah, and Christ, who each communed closely with the Father.

mc.stem: The lesson gives three reasons God is sometimes silent. Which set is correct?
options: Because He is angry, tired, or far away
Because we are unworthy, weak, or new believers
Because we must experience Him, we haven't tuned in, or we have turned away
Because the times are evil, the church is cold, or prayer is weak
mc.why: God may be silent for three reasons: we must learn to experience Him, we haven't tuned in, or we have turned away.

mc.stem: Why, according to John 4:24, can our five physical senses not reach God?
options: Because only prophets can sense Him
Because God is far away in heaven
Because God is Spirit and must be worshiped in spirit and truth
mc.why: God is Spirit (John 4:24), so the five physical senses cannot reach Him; He is known in spirit and truth.

mc.stem: What did Eli teach young Samuel to say when he heard the voice again?
options: "Speak, LORD, for Your servant is listening"
mc.why: Eli taught Samuel the posture of hearing God: 'Speak, LORD, for Your servant is listening.'

mc.stem: In the story of the man born blind who received sight, why was he terrified when the bandages came off?
options: His brain had never processed sight and the flood of sensation overwhelmed him
He could not believe it had worked
The light hurt his eyes permanently
mc.why: The man born blind was terrified because his brain had never processed sight — learning to perceive God takes time too.

mc.stem: As a teenager, what did Catherine Marshall surrender to God?
options: Her dreams — college and the man she would one day marry
mc.why: As a teenager Catherine Marshall surrendered her dreams — college and marriage — and learned to trust God in the silence.

mc.stem: According to the lesson, what is the grace often hidden inside God's silence?
options: It is a punishment for doubt
It is a sign He has left us
It is one of His ways of getting our attention and drawing us toward Him
It means our prayers were wrong
mc.why: God's silence is often grace: one of His ways of getting our attention and drawing us toward Himself.

mc.stem: The lesson says only one person ever heard the total silence of God. Who, and when?
options: Jesus on the cross, crying "Why have You forsaken Me?"
mc.why: Only one person ever heard the total silence of God — Jesus on the cross, crying 'Why have You forsaken Me?' — so we never need to.

mc.stem: Which verse does the lesson hold up as the key to hearing God through silence?
options: "Be still, and know that I am God" (Psalm 46:10)
mc.why: The key to hearing God through silence is Psalm 46:10: 'Be still, and know that I am God.'

mc.stem: According to the lesson, how does God usually speak?
options: In a still, small voice easily drowned out by the world's noise
mc.why: God usually speaks in a still, small voice, easily drowned out by the noise of the world.

mc.stem: In the ice house story, how did the little boy find the lost watch when the men could not?
options: He asked where it was last seen
He lay down quietly and listened for the ticking
mc.why: The boy found the lost watch by lying down quietly and listening for the ticking — some things are heard only in stillness.

mc.stem: The student who could hear a cricket above the roar of Fifth Avenue illustrates what about hearing God?
options: That God shouts louder than the world
That cities are too noisy for faith
That we hear what our ears are tuned to; we must train our hearts to God's voice
That only some people can hear God
mc.why: The cricket heard above Fifth Avenue shows we hear what our ears are tuned to; we must train our hearts to God's voice.

mc.stem: According to the lesson, how can we tune our hearts to God's frequency each day?
options: By asking each morning, "Lord, what is before me to do today?" and then listening
mc.why: We tune in each day by asking, 'Lord, what is before me to do today?' and then listening for His answer.

mc.stem: When Adam sinned and God called, "Adam, where are you?", what does the lesson say this shows?
options: That God had lost track of Adam
That God was seeking him; it was Adam who had hidden
That God was angry and shouting

sa.prompt: Describe the pain of God's silence as the lesson introduces it, and how Psalm 28:1 voices it.
sa.model: The lesson introduces the pain of God's silence with the picture of a screen going dark when the signal is lost, leaving only emptiness where a voice should be. We feel that same disorientation when God seems silent, when we pray and hear nothing. Psalm 28:1 voices it directly: "Do not be silent to me, lest, if You are silent to me, I become like those who go down to the pit." The psalmist treats God's silence as a matter of life and death. The lesson takes that cry seriously rather than dismissing it, because the silence of God is one of the hardest trials of faith.

sa.prompt: Explain the first reason God is silent: we must experience Him. Why do the five senses not reach God?
sa.model: The first reason God is sometimes silent is that we must learn to experience Him, not merely to gather information. The lesson points to John 4:24, that God is Spirit and must be worshiped in spirit and truth; because God is Spirit, our five physical senses cannot reach Him. We cannot see, hear, or touch Him the way we do the material world. So His apparent silence may be teaching us to know Him in a deeper way, through faith and spiritual communion rather than physical proof. The silence presses us beyond our senses into a real, spiritual relationship with the living God.

sa.prompt: Retell the account of Samuel in the temple and explain what it teaches about hearing God.
sa.model: When the boy Samuel heard a voice in the night, he ran to Eli, thinking the old priest had called him. Eli realized it was the LORD and taught Samuel to answer, "Speak, LORD, for Your servant is listening." The account teaches that hearing God begins with a listening, available heart, ready to respond rather than to demand. Samuel did not conjure the voice; he made himself available to it. So with us: we learn to hear God not by forcing Him to speak but by quieting ourselves before Him and saying, in effect, "Speak, Lord; I am listening," then attending to His Word.

sa.prompt: Retell the Catherine Marshall story and explain what it shows about surrender and God's silence as grace.
sa.model: As a teenager Catherine Marshall surrendered her dreams to God, including college and the man she would one day marry, laying down what she most wanted before Him. The story shows that God's silences are often the place where surrender is learned, and that His silence can itself be grace. Rather than abandoning her, God was using the silence to draw her closer and to teach her to trust Him with her future. The account reframes silence: it is not necessarily God withdrawing, but often one of His ways of deepening our surrender and getting our full attention.

sa.prompt: Explain the second reason God is silent: we haven't tuned in. Use Psalm 46:10 and the still small voice.
sa.model: The second reason God is silent is that we have not tuned in. God usually speaks in a still, small voice, easily drowned out by the noise of the world and our own hurry. Psalm 46:10 gives the remedy: "Be still, and know that I am God." We must quiet ourselves, slow down, and make space to listen, or we will miss what He is saying. The silence may not be God refusing to speak, but our failure to be still enough to hear. Learning to be quiet before Him is essential to hearing the gentle voice that the world's clamor so easily covers.

sa.prompt: Retell the ice house story and the Fifth Avenue cricket story, and explain what each teaches about listening for God.
sa.model: In the ice house story, men searching for a lost watch could not find it amid their own noise, until a boy lay down quietly and heard it ticking. In the Fifth Avenue story, a visitor heard a cricket above the city's roar because his ear was tuned to that sound. Both teach that we hear what we are listening for and what we are still enough to catch. To hear God we must quiet the inner noise and tune our hearts to His voice. The problem is rarely that God has stopped speaking; it is that we have not made ourselves still and attentive enough to hear.

sa.prompt: Explain the third reason God is silent: we have turned away. Use Adam and the strep-throat illustration.
sa.model: The third reason God is silent is that we have turned away through sin. When God called, "Adam, where are you?", He was seeking Adam; it was Adam who had hidden himself after sinning. Sin makes us hide and breaks the fellowship in which we hear God. The strep-throat illustration shows how this works: an untreated infection spreads and can stop up the ears, just as unchecked sin spreads through the soul and stops up the ears of faith until we no longer hear God clearly. The silence in this case is a summons to deal honestly with sin and return to Him.

sa.prompt: Explain the law of sowing and reaping and the law of chastening, and how each relates to God's silence.
sa.model: The lesson distinguishes two laws. The law of sowing and reaping is universal: everyone, believer or not, reaps the natural consequences of what they sow. The law of chastening is different; it applies only to God's children, for the Lord disciplines those He loves, as a father corrects his sons. Both can lie behind a season of God's silence. We may be reaping painful consequences, or we may be experiencing the loving discipline of a Father who wants to draw us back. Either way, the silence is not meaningless; it calls us to examine our lives and return to close fellowship with God.

sa.prompt: Explain William Barclay's point about repentance, and the prayer of Psalm 139:23 for a season of silence.
sa.model: William Barclay said that real repentance always involves two movements: a turning FROM something and a turning TOWARD something, away from sin and back to God. Mere regret is not enough; repentance changes direction. For a season when God seems silent, the lesson offers the prayer of Psalm 139:23, "Search me, O God, and know my heart... see if there is any wicked way in me." Rather than blaming God for the silence, we invite Him to show us anything that needs to be turned from, so that whatever has come between us can be confessed and the fellowship in which we hear Him can be restored.

sa.prompt: According to the close of the lesson, how should a believer respond in a season when God seems silent?
sa.model: According to the close of the lesson, a believer in a season of God's silence should not panic or conclude that God has abandoned him, but respond with quiet trust and self-examination. He should be still before God, listen for the still small voice, and pray to be searched, dealing honestly with any sin. He should remember that only Jesus on the cross ever bore the total silence of God, crying "why have You forsaken Me?", so that we never have to. The silence is not the absence of God but often His way of drawing us deeper, and faith waits on Him, trusting He is present even when unheard.
